Background Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) is a major transboundary viral pathogen of small ruminants and causes substantial economic losses in endemic regions. The hemagglutinin (H) protein mediates receptor recognition and host-cell attachment and is an important target for vaccine development. This study applied an integrated computational framework to identify conserved immunogenic regions within the PPRV H protein. Methods A total of 609 amino acid residues were analyzed using multiple sequence alignment, entropy-based conservation profiling, conservation-aware epitope prediction, validation against experimentally characterized immune determinants, structural mapping, and computational candidate ranking. Predicted epitopes were compared with reported immune determinants and integrated with conservation and structural data. Results The workflow identified 9 high-confidence B-cell epitopes and 25 putative T-cell epitope candidates distributed throughout the H protein sequence. The strongest predicted B-cell epitope was localized within residues 576–588, whereas the highest-ranked putative T-cell epitope candidate corresponded to residues 36–44. Conservation analysis identified 412 residues with conservation scores greater than 0.9. Validation against experimentally characterized immune determinants demonstrated agreement with previously reported immune determinants. Structural mapping revealed clustering of conserved residues, predicted epitopes, experimentally characterized immune regions, and overlap hotspots. Computational candidate ranking identified residues 399–407 (SGPWSEGRI) as the highest-ranked region. Conclusions Integrated computational analysis combining conservation profiling, immune epitope prediction, structural interpretation, validation against experimentally characterized immune determinants, and computational candidate prioritization identified biologically relevant immune targets within the PPRV H protein. The identified hotspots represent promising candidates for future experimental validation and vaccine development.
